This code contains a critical uninitialized memory usage vulnerability that stems from exclusive reliance on debug-only assertion macros for input validation that are stripped from production release builds. This code contains a critical improper access control vulnerability rooted in flawed path assignment prior to security permission validation. A local unprivileged attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a carefully constructed path that points to a restricted nested cgroup subdirectory, bypassing intended access controls that would otherwise block the directory creation operation. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to create unauthorized cgroup directories in restricted areas of the cgroup filesystem, enabling resource hijacking, denial of service, or even privilege escalation against other unprivileged system users.

This code contains a local unprivileged denial of service vulnerability caused by a user-triggerable kernel BUG assertion that leads to a system-wide panic. A local attacker with the ability to create or modify a custom dns resolver key can populate the relevant payload field with a crafted non-error value to trigger this flaw, leading the seq_file output to expose arbitrary unintended values from kernel memory instead of the expected error code or key datalen value. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to corrupt adjacent stack memory, hijack control flow, and execute arbitrary code in the context of the running process.

An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a maliciously crafted ELF binary with carefully constructed large note name or description size values that bypass the existing partial checks, leading to reads of data outside the allocated bounds of the vbuf heap buffer. Successful exploitation allows an attacker to leak sensitive adjacent memory contents from the running process or induce a fatal segmentation fault to cause a denial of service condition on the targeted system.

This code contains a disabled security policy enforcement vulnerability where the check for minimum password lifetime is fully excluded from compilation via an #if 0 preprocessor directive. The root cause is that the critical conditional logic that validates if the elapsed time since the last password change meets the configured pol.pw_min_life threshold is omitted from the build, so the KADM5_PASS_TOOSOON error that blocks premature password changes is never returned to callers. An authenticated attacker with access to modify a target principal's credentials can trigger this flaw by initiating repeated password or random key generation operations in rapid succession, bypassing the intended enforced minimum password age policy entirely. This allows the attacker to evade password history reuse restrictions, subvert audit trail integrity, and violate organizational security compliance requirements that mandate minimum password lifetime controls for Kerberos principals.

This code contains an integer overflow and resultant heap out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the associative array shortcut duplication logic. The root cause is that the code derives the keylen value directly from the unvalidated shortcut->skip_to_level field, using it to calculate the total allocation size for the new shortcut and the length of the trailing memcpy operation without performing any upper bound checks to ensure the derived keylen cannot exceed safe limits. An attacker can trigger this flaw by inserting a maliciously crafted shortcut entry with an excessively large skip_to_level value into the target associative array, then initiating the garbage collection routine to process the corrupted entry. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to leak sensitive adjacent heap memory contents, corrupt unrelated heap metadata, and ultimately achieve full privilege escalation on the affected system.

This C implementation of ZSTD_buildCTable contains an unvalidated out-of-bounds read vulnerability that can be triggered when processing the set_rle or set_compressed encoding type cases. The root cause is the absence of input validation for the user-controlled nbSeq parameter before indexing into the codeTable buffer, as the code directly accesses codeTable[0] in the set_rle case and codeTable[nbSeq-1] in the set_compressed case with no check that nbSeq is at a minimum value of 1. A remote attacker can supply a crafted compressed payload that sets nbSeq to a value of 0, which causes the index calculation nbSeq-1 to underflow to a very large unsigned integer that reads arbitrary memory outside the bounds of the codeTable allocation. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows an attacker to leak sensitive adjacent stack or heap memory contents, bypass expected memory isolation protections, and potentially achieve arbitrary code execution by corrupting adjacent critical program state.

This code exhibits an improper access control ordering vulnerability where the size validation operation invoked via inode_newsize_ok runs before any checks that verify the requesting caller holds sufficient privileges to modify the target inode. The root cause of this flaw is that the ATTR_SIZE handling block is positioned ahead of all permission validation logic for inode modification, so the size processing routine executes fully even for unprivileged callers that will later be rejected with an EPERM error. A local attacker can trigger this vulnerability by repeatedly sending inode change requests with the ATTR_SIZE flag set and custom size values, without possessing the required privileges to alter the target inode. This can allow the attacker to trigger expensive side effects inside inode_newsize_ok such as excessive page cache eviction or repeated resource allocation attempts, leading to a reliable local denial of service that degrades system performance or crashes the affected kernel.

This code contains a critical unprotected double initialization vulnerability that affects the lifecycle management of the PulseAudioMixer component. The root cause is that the InitSync function implements no pre-check to confirm the instance has not already started or completed an initialization sequence before calling InitThread and PulseAudioInit in immediate succession. An attacker who can trigger multiple concurrent or sequential calls to InitSync on the same PulseAudioMixer instance before the first initialization flow finishes can force overlapping execution of the underlying thread and audio system setup routines. This can lead to uninitialized memory access, race condition induced heap corruption, unexpected process crashes, or even arbitrary code execution within the context of the privileged audio service process.

This code contains a critical null pointer dereference vulnerability stemming from the use of debug-only DCHECK assertions that are omitted in production release builds. The root cause is that the only validation for the non-null status of inherit_from->GetSecurityContext() and its associated ContentSecurityPolicy pointer is placed inside a DCHECK statement, which does not execute in non-debug builds, leaving no runtime checks to ensure these pointers are valid before they are dereferenced to assign policy_to_inherit. A remote attacker can trigger this vulnerability by manipulating frame hierarchy or opener properties to create a valid execution path where either the security context or its linked content security policy object is null, leading to an unexpected access of invalid memory. Successful exploitation of this flaw will result in a browser process crash, unintended circumvention of content security policy protections, and in some scenarios may allow an attacker to achieve arbitrary code execution within the privileged browser sandbox to run unauthorized malicious code.

The identified security vulnerability is missing bounds validation for the pointsOfInterest input values processed in the SetMediaTrackConstraints function. The root cause is that while the code implements explicit range checks for all other numeric camera parameters including exposure compensation, color temperature, iso, brightness, and contrast, it completely omits any validation that the x and y coordinate values extracted from the Point2D sequence are within the valid min and max ranges defined in the device's stored capabilities_ structure. A remote attacker can trigger this flaw by crafting a malicious media track constraints payload that passes arbitrary out-of-bounds floating point values for the pointsOfInterest x and y fields while satisfying all other existing constraint validation checks. Successful exploitation can lead to unexpected camera driver behavior, out-of-bounds memory access in the underlying privileged system camera service code, persistent denial of service of the video capture pipeline, or arbitrary code execution within the elevated media process that handles low level camera hardware controls.

This C code contains a critical unvalidated out-of-bounds memory access vulnerability rooted in the use of assert macros for all critical array boundary checks, which are completely stripped from compiled binaries when the standard NDEBUG flag is enabled for release builds. The binary search logic for cue points performs pointer arithmetic on the m_cue_points array using the user-controlled m_count value to define the upper bound jj, and no non-debug runtime validation exists to ensure calculated intermediate pointers k, i and j never access memory outside the actual allocated bounds of the m_cue_points buffer. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a specially crafted malformed media file that sets the m_count field to a value far larger than the actual number of allocated entries in the m_cue_points array, causing the binary search loop to read adjacent unintended heap memory locations. Successful exploitation can lead to sensitive information disclosure of adjacent heap data, unexpected program denial of service via segmentation fault, or even arbitrary code execution if the out-of-bounds read retrieves a corrupted or attacker-controlled pointer that is later dereferenced when calling the CuePoint Find method.
There is no vulnerability.

This UDF file system kernel routine contains a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability that arises from insufficient validation of untrusted on-disk input values. The root cause is that the 8-bit lengthFileIdent field stored in the struct fileIdentDesc, referenced by the local variable lfi, is read directly from unvalidated disk data and used as a length parameter for memcpy operations targeting the heap-allocated fname buffer, which is allocated with a fixed size of UDF_NAME_LEN without any prior bounds check to ensure lfi does not exceed this allocated size. A local attacker can trigger this vulnerability by creating a malicious UDF disk image with a tampered fileIdentDesc that sets the lengthFileIdent value larger than UDF_NAME_LEN, then mounting the malicious image on a target system. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to write arbitrary amounts of out-of-bounds data to the kernel heap, leading to adjacent kernel memory corruption, full system denial of service, arbitrary kernel code execution, and local privilege escalation to root user privileges.

This hb_buffer_clear function contains an unvalidated pointer access vulnerability that can lead to unintended null pointer dereference. The root cause is that the function directly writes to multiple members of the input hb_buffer_t pointer such as buffer->have_output and buffer->len without performing any prior validation to confirm the pointer points to a valid allocated memory region. A remote or local attacker can trigger this vulnerability by passing a null or uninitialized pointer value as the buffer argument to the function during normal API usage flows. Exploitation of this issue will result in immediate abnormal program termination and denial of service, and may enable arbitrary memory corruption and full code execution if an attacker supplies a carefully controlled invalid pointer value that maps to a writable memory address outside the intended hb_buffer_t structure.

This code contains a critical use-after-free vulnerability rooted in improper lifetime management of the local scoped_refptr NaClIPCAdapter instance declared within the params.enable_ipc_proxy conditional block. The code assigns the result of ipc_adapter.get()->MakeNaClDesc() directly to the args->initial_ipc_desc field, then exits the conditional block where the ipc_adapter variable is declared, triggering automatic destruction of the NaClIPCAdapter instance and freeing all associated memory before args is passed to NaClChromeMainStart. An attacker controlling the untrusted params input to this function can set enable_ipc_proxy to true to trigger this dangling pointer condition, allowing them to manipulate freed memory contents before the subsequent NaClChromeMainStart call references the now-invalid initial_ipc_desc pointer. This can lead to arbitrary read and write access in the privileged browser process memory space, enabling full remote code execution and complete system compromise under the browser's running user context.

The identified security vulnerability is an incomplete error handling and uninitialized return value flaw present in the truncated implementation of the create_qp_common function. The root cause is that the function initializes multiple synchronization primitives at its start and allocates multiple kernel resources during execution, but cuts off immediately after the final if (err) check without defining any subsequent logic to return a valid error code or clean up already initialized resources. A local privileged or unprivileged attacker with access to the InfiniBand udata interface can trigger this flaw by sending specially crafted input values that cause the create_user_qp or create_kernel_qp subroutines to return a non-zero error status. This flaw will cause the function to return an undefined uninitialized stack value to the caller, leak sensitive kernel memory contents, or leave reference counts and synchronization objects in an inconsistent state that can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation or denial of service on the target host.

This code contains an unvalidated pointer dereference vulnerability that arises from directly dereferencing the return value of clip_tree.Node without any prior null check. The root cause is the complete lack of runtime error handling for a potential failure of the preceding clip_tree.Insert operation, which can leave the underlying ClipTree in an inconsistent state where no valid node exists at the requested ID, causing the Node method to return a null pointer. An attacker who can trigger memory exhaustion or heap corruption in the ClipTree backing storage during the Insert call can force the code to access unintended memory when initializing the clip_node structure. This flaw can lead to a critical process crash resulting in a denial of service condition for the host graphics rendering application, and in severe cases may allow an attacker to execute arbitrary malicious code by manipulating the contents of the invalid accessed memory region.

This code contains an integer overflow vulnerability in the bounds validation logic for the incoming RNDIS set message buffer. The root cause is that the unsigned 32-bit addition of bufoffs and buflen in the conditional check bufoffs + buflen > length can wrap around to a small value if the sum exceeds the maximum value for a 32-bit unsigned integer, allowing the bounds check to incorrectly pass even when the combined offset and length exceed the actual valid input buffer size. An attacker can trigger this flaw by sending a malicious RNDIS set message that sets InformationBufferOffset and InformationBufferLength to values whose sum wraps past 32 bits, bypassing the length validation entirely. This leads to a subsequent out-of-bounds memory read when the calculated pointer bufoffs + (uint8_t *) buf is passed to the ndis_set function, which can leak sensitive adjacent heap memory, trigger a system crash and denial of service, or enable arbitrary code execution through misinterpreted adjacent memory values passed as unvalidated NDIS OID parameters.

This mutt_b64_decode function contains an unvalidated output buffer write vulnerability that arises from the absence of any input parameter specifying the allocated size of the destination out buffer. The root cause is the complete lack of bounds checking on writes to the out pointer, as the function sequentially writes decoded bytes and increments the out address without ever verifying it remains within the bounds of the reserved memory region. An attacker can trigger this flaw by passing a long, properly formatted base64 input string that the existing validation logic accepts, leading the loop to process successive 4-byte input chunks and write more decoded output bytes than the destination buffer can accommodate. Exploitation of this issue allows an attacker to corrupt adjacent stack or heap memory, leading to arbitrary code execution, unintended disclosure of sensitive in-memory data, or unexpected process termination that results in a denial of service condition.

This code contains a critical NULL pointer dereference vulnerability rooted in incomplete initialization of the or_circ variable, which is only assigned a valid non-NULL value if the input circuit is not marked as an origin circuit. When an attacker sends a valid RELAY_COMMAND_BEGIN_DIR cell targeting an origin circuit that passes the earlier circuit purpose validation check, execution proceeds to the tor_assert(or_circ) call that enforces a non-NULL or_circ value, triggering an immediate program abort. This flaw can be exploited by a remote network attacker that transmits a crafted Tor relay cell to a target Tor instance, resulting in a complete denial of service for the affected node. The earlier protocol validation steps for begindir requests do not exclude origin circuits, so the malicious cell bypasses all prior checks to reach the unprotected assertion without prior rejection.

This CIPSO v4 option validation function contains an integer wrap-around vulnerability that leads to out-of-bounds memory access when processing maliciously formatted IP options. The root cause is that the loop counter opt_iter is declared as unsigned char, an 8-bit type that can only hold values from 0 to 255, so repeated increments by tag_len will cause the variable to silently overflow and reset to a small positive value once the total offset exceeds 255. An attacker can trigger this flaw by constructing a spoofed CIPSO option with a sequence of valid recognized security tags whose combined length exceeds 255 bytes, so the wrapped opt_iter value remains less than the 8-bit opt_len value to keep the main while loop executing past the intended buffer bounds. This causes the tag pointer to be incremented outside the valid range of the sk_buff associated option data, enabling unauthorized disclosure of adjacent kernel memory contents, arbitrary kernel memory reads, or a fatal system denial of service via unhandled page fault.

This GpuChannel constructor implementation contains an unvalidated raw pointer misuse vulnerability tied to the incoming share_group parameter. The root cause of the issue is that the code directly assigns a non-null caller-provided share_group pointer to the class member share_group_ without validating that the pointer references a valid, properly allocated gfx::GLShareGroup instance, and does not increment any associated reference count to ensure the pointed-to object remains in memory for the full lifetime of the GpuChannel object. A local or remote attacker that can influence the value of the share_group parameter can supply a dangling, arbitrary, or corrupted memory address as this pointer value to trigger unintended memory access operations during subsequent use of the share_group_ member. Successful exploitation of this flaw can result in out of bounds memory reads and writes, arbitrary code execution, or unexpected process termination leading to a denial of service scenario.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds write vulnerability rooted in incomplete integer overflow validation of user-provided DRM submission arguments. The root cause is that the existing 32-bit offset wrap checks do not account for the fact that the aligned offset calculations can produce a final exec_size value that is smaller than the total combined size of the three user-supplied buffers copied via copy_from_user, allowing the user to pass large carefully crafted size values that pass the explicit overflow checks but exceed the actual size of the GEM buffer object allocated via vc4_bo_create. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying malicious values for bin_cl_size, shader_rec_size, and uniforms_size to the DRM VC4 submit IOCTL, which will cause the subsequent validation operations to write data well beyond the end of the bounds of the allocated graphics buffer. Successful exploitation of this flaw allows a local attacker to perform arbitrary kernel memory writes, escalate privileges to root, or execute arbitrary code with the full permissions of the running kernel.

This code implements an autofill suggestion population routine that lacks proper validation of untrusted input suggestion entries supplied via the input_suggestions parameter. The root cause of the vulnerability is the complete absence of allowed-list validation for the frontend_id field of incoming Suggestion objects, which are copied directly into the local suggestions vector without sanitization before being processed for display in the autofill popup. A remote attacker who can inject a maliciously constructed input_suggestions vector with arbitrary, out-of-range frontend_id values can trigger unintended control flows when the suggestions are passed to the ShowAutofillPopup routine, as the unvalidated IDs may be used as indices into internal action dispatch tables for popup item selection. Successful exploitation of this flaw can lead to arbitrary memory read and write operations, unexpected privilege escalation within the browser process, or even remote code execution under the browser’s security context.

This hcom_client_init implementation contains multiple security vulnerabilities stemming from insufficient input validation. The code does not validate that the input pointers server_path, client_path and the output pointer p_hdl are non-NULL before dereferencing them with strlen and the final assignment to *p_hdl, so an attacker that passes any of these pointers as NULL will trigger an immediate application crash to achieve a denial of service. The code also performs no checks on the signed integer max_data_len parameter to confirm it holds a positive non-negative value, so an attacker that supplies a negative max_data_len value will cause the value to be cast to an excessively large unsigned size when passed to malloc, leading to unexpected allocation failures, memory exhaustion, or potential memory corruption in subsequent buffer handling operations.

This code contains an untrusted input validation vulnerability that arises from the direct assignment of values retrieved via the GET_PARAM macro to internal state variables with no accompanying sanitization or bounds checking. The root cause is the complete absence of type and range validation for the four retrieved parameters, as the code assumes all values returned by GET_PARAM are valid, expected, and safe for later use in the video transform operations the surrounding code implements. A remote or local attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying maliciously crafted unexpected values through the exposed parameter input interface, such as negative size values, invalid pointer references, or out-of-range indices for the transform function pointers. Successful exploitation of this flaw can lead to severe memory safety violations including invalid pointer dereference, out-of-bounds read or write operations, sensitive process memory disclosure, and even full arbitrary code execution in the context of the vulnerable process.

This MPEG4 media parsing code contains an uncontrolled recursion vulnerability that leads to stack exhaustion. The root cause is that the parseChunk function recursively invokes itself to process nested MPEG4 atoms without enforcing any maximum upper bound on the depth parameter, even though existing chunk size validation allows for valid nested chunks to be placed at arbitrarily deep levels of the file structure. An attacker can trigger this flaw by constructing a malicious MPEG4 file with a long chain of properly formatted nested chunks that pass all existing input validation checks. Successful exploitation will exhaust the process's call stack, leading to a critical denial of service condition, and in some unhardened execution environments may allow for remote arbitrary code execution via unhandled stack memory corruption.
There is no vulnerability.

This code contains an unvalidated user-controlled buffer length vulnerability leading to an out-of-bounds memory write. The root cause is that the function directly casts the caller-provided msg->msg_name pointer to a struct sockaddr_ax25 pointer and writes multiple fields to this structure, without first verifying that the caller-set msg->msg_namelen value is at least equal to the size of the target struct sockaddr_ax25. A local attacker with access to the configured network socket can trigger this flaw by passing a msghdr with a msg_name buffer that points to a small allocated region with a msg_namelen value smaller than the size of struct sockaddr_ax25, which causes the subsequent writes to sax->sax25_family and the sax25_call field to overflow the bounds of the intended destination buffer. Successful exploitation of this issue can allow an attacker to corrupt adjacent kernel or user memory, leading to arbitrary code execution, privilege escalation, or system wide denial of service.

This DTLS record processing implementation contains an insufficient version validation vulnerability for the first incoming packet, as the strict full version equality check that compares the parsed version value against s->version is guarded by the if (!s->first_packet) conditional, so no full version validation runs for the first received DTLS record. The root cause is that the remaining partial version mask check only validates the high 8 bits of the 16-bit version field, leaving the low 8 bits of the parsed version value unvalidated for the first packet, allowing an attacker to inject a crafted DTLS record with arbitrary values in the low byte of the version field. A remote unauthenticated attacker can trigger this flaw by sending a malformed DTLS initial record with a mismatched low version byte directly to a listening DTLS service, bypassing intended version enforcement logic. Successful exploitation can lead to unexpected record parsing behavior, out of bounds memory reads during subsequent cryptographic operations, or even remote code execution depending on how the unvalidated version value is used later in the TLS stack processing flow.

This MKV parsing implementation contains a critical memory safety vulnerability stemming from the exclusive use of assert macros for all critical bounds and value validation checks, which are fully compiled out in non-debug production builds with no corresponding runtime validation logic. The root cause is the lack of a runtime check to confirm that the long long value size_ does not exceed the maximum representable positive value of the native long type before the cast operation that assigns size_ to buflen_, allowing for unintended negative values or invalid length values to propagate through the rest of the function. An attacker can trigger this flaw by constructing a malicious MKV media file that sets a very large element size value far larger than the maximum 32-bit signed integer limit, which will bypass all omitted assert checks and result in an invalid negative or undersized buflen_ value being used for heap allocation and subsequent read operations. This flaw can lead to severe heap memory corruption, out of bounds memory access, unexpected program crashes, and potential remote arbitrary code execution when processing the malicious media file.

This code contains an unenforced thread safety validation vulnerability that affects production release builds of the application. The root cause is that the thread validity check implemented via DCHECK(CalledOnValidThread()) is a debug-only assertion that is fully compiled out of non-debug release binaries, leaving no runtime enforcement that the RegisterIds function is invoked exclusively on its designated valid thread. An attacker capable of triggering execution of this method on an unexpected unvetted thread can induce unsynchronized concurrent access to shared class member variables including registered_ids_, ticl_state_, and registration_manager_, triggering exploitable race conditions that can lead to unexpected state corruption, invalid pointer dereference, memory disclosure, or arbitrary code execution within the target application’s running process.

This code contains an unvalidated pointer dereference vulnerability that occurs when the parent_widget_ member is null, as the implementation directly dereferences the delegate_ pointer without first verifying that it is not null. The root cause is the complete omission of a null check for the delegate_ variable prior to accessing its container_view method in the fallback return path. An attacker can trigger this flaw by manipulating the application UI lifecycle to force the parent_widget_ value to null while the delegate_ pointer has been freed or left uninitialized, leading to attempted read access of an invalid memory address. Successful exploitation will result in a critical process crash that causes a persistent denial of service condition, and under unfavorable memory layout circumstances may allow an attacker to execute arbitrary malicious code within the context of the privileged running application process.

This WebKit JavaScript binding code contains an unvalidated pointer dereference vulnerability stemming from improper handling of the third user-supplied function argument. The root cause is that the code assigns the integer output of the toint conversion of the third JavaScript parameter directly to an int pointer b, with no validation that the resulting integer value refers to a valid, process-accessible memory location, even after the incomplete type check for the argument. A remote attacker can supply a carefully crafted arbitrary integer value as the third argument to this exposed JavaScript strictFunction, which will be treated as a raw memory address and passed directly to the underlying native C++ implementation of the TestObj strictFunction method. This can be exploited to trigger out of bounds memory read or write operations, enabling the attacker to leak sensitive process memory, corrupt critical runtime data structures, and ultimately achieve full remote code execution within the context of the running JavaScript engine process.

This hstore_from_array implementation contains an integer overflow vulnerability that leads to exploitable heap buffer overflow. The root cause is the absence of overflow validation for the allocation size calculation in the line pairs = palloc(count * sizeof(Pairs)), allowing an extremely large count value derived from a high element count input array to wrap around the limits of the signed integer type and produce a far smaller allocation size than required. An attacker can trigger this flaw by submitting a specially crafted array with an extremely high valid element count that passes all existing dimension parity and structure checks, resulting in an undersized heap buffer being allocated to store the Pairs structure entries. The subsequent loop that populates entries in the pairs array will write out of the bounds of the allocated buffer, leading to arbitrary heap memory corruption that an attacker can exploit to execute arbitrary code in the context of the backend database process or trigger a complete server crash for a high severity denial of service condition.

This code contains an invalid pointer dereference vulnerability in the V_ASN1_BOOLEAN case handling logic. The root cause is that the code assigns tbool as a cast of pval directly instead of dereferencing the double pointer pval first, which means tbool points to the memory holding the ASN1_VALUE pointer rather than the actual underlying ASN1_BOOLEAN value intended for access. An attacker can trigger this flaw by processing a malformed ASN1 encoded boolean input that reaches this code path, leading to reads of unintended adjacent stack or heap memory values instead of the actual boolean data. This vulnerability can lead to incorrect ASN1 serialization output, unexpected program behavior, or arbitrary out of bounds memory access that may enable sensitive information disclosure or remote code execution depending on the surrounding memory layout.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds write vulnerability stemming from missing validation of the untrusted integer field parameter passed to the copy_fields function. The root cause is that the code directly calculates the destination pointer offset as field*dst->linesize[plane] without checking that the value of field is restricted to the only two valid values 0 and 1 required for correct interleaved field copy operations. An attacker exploiting this vulnerability can provide a maliciously crafted media file that sets the field parameter to a negative or very large non-permitted value, leading to generation of an invalid out-of-bounds memory address that is written to during the av_image_copy_plane operation. Successful exploitation can result in arbitrary memory corruption, unexpected program termination due to a segmentation fault, or full remote code execution depending on the layout of adjacent memory and the permissions of the running process.

This code contains a critical shared state race condition vulnerability stemming from the use of a non-blocking mutex try locker that does not enforce exclusive consistent access to all mutable shared media element state. The root cause is that the MutexTryLocker can successfully acquire the lock at a point where concurrent execution on another thread has already initiated deallocation or reconfiguration of the mediaElement, audioSourceProvider, or associated resampler state, with no post-lock validation to confirm all referenced objects remain valid for the full duration of the audio processing operation. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by manipulating rapid media element load and unload events across separate threads to time execution of the process function exactly when the target media element is being torn down, leading to a dangling pointer dereference when the code invokes provider->provideInput or the resampler process method. Successful exploitation of this issue can result in unexpected program termination, out of bounds memory access, or full remote code execution within the security context of the running media processing service.

This C code for the PHP Phar extension addEmptyDir method contains an insufficient path validation security vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass restrictions on creating directories inside the reserved magic ".phar" directory. The root cause of the flaw is that the implemented check only verifies that the first five bytes of the user-supplied dirname do not match the ".phar" sequence, rather than scanning every individual path segment across the full provided directory path to detect any occurrence of the restricted directory name. An attacker can trigger the vulnerability by submitting a nested directory path such as "test/.phar/evil" that does not start with the ".phar" sequence, which evades the existing guard check and allows the underlying phar_mkdir function to create directories within the protected reserved archive region. Successful exploitation of this flaw allows an attacker to tamper with internal Phar archive metadata structures, bypass archive integrity checks, and execute arbitrary malicious code when the manipulated Phar archive is parsed by a vulnerable PHP runtime.

This code contains multiple unvalidated out-of-bounds read vulnerabilities during processing of ID3 album art frames across all supported ID3 version variants. The root cause is that the code performs unsafe string and memory comparison operations directly on untrusted frame data before validating that the required offset ranges fit within the declared frame size, including calling strlen on the MIME string offset for ID3v2.3 and ID3v2.4 frames without confirming a null terminator exists inside the valid data range, and performing 3-byte memcmp operations on the MIME identifier offset for older ID3 versions without confirming the frame holds at least 4 bytes of data. A remote attacker can supply a specially constructed media file with manipulated truncated ID3 album art frames to trigger these flaws, leading to disclosure of adjacent heap memory contents, unexpected application crash via access to unmapped memory, or potential arbitrary code execution via leakage or corruption of adjacent heap metadata.

The primary security vulnerability in this code is unvalidated and unescaped user-controlled content injection into structured XML output. The root cause occurs because the function directly passes the raw tag->bit_name and tag->bit_val values to the fprintf call that builds XML attribute strings, with no logic to escape XML-reserved metacharacters such as double quotes, angle brackets, or ampersands that alter XML document structure. An attacker who can manipulate device tag metadata can craft malicious tag names or values to break out of the defined attribute boundaries, inject arbitrary additional XML content, or corrupt the output file. When this generated XML file is parsed by a privileged system utility, the attacker may trigger unexpected parsing behavior, execute arbitrary unintended code paths, or escalate privileges on the target system.

This DeviceTokenFetcher::StopAutoRetry implementation contains a critical unprotected race condition leading to a use-after-free security vulnerability. The root cause is the complete lack of thread synchronization around the paired operations of scheduler_->CancelDelayedWork() and backend_.reset(), which does not guarantee that all pending or in-flight delayed work tasks owned by the scheduler have fully exited their execution paths before the backend_ instance is deallocated. An attacker who can trigger concurrent execution of StopAutoRetry and any active delayed work task that references the backend_ object can force the backend_ to be freed while the scheduler task still holds a valid dereferenceable pointer to the now-deallocated memory region. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can yield arbitrary memory read and write access, enable remote code execution in the context of the host process, or cause a persistent unhandled crash that results in full denial of service for the device token fetching workflow.

This code contains an unvalidated bounds arithmetic vulnerability that occurs in the final protocol handling switch block where the code performs unguarded arithmetic on the packet pointer p and the associated length fields l2info.length and l2info.caplen. The root cause is that there are no pre-flight checks to verify that operations such as p + 1, p - 1, l2info.length - 1, and l2info.caplen + 1 do not produce out-of-range values that exceed the bounds of the input packet buffer or underflow to negative values that wrap to large unsigned integers. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a specially crafted malicious Juniper MFR packet capture that sets l2info.length or l2info.caplen to 0, or positions the p pointer at the start of the input packet buffer, to force execution of the vulnerable arithmetic paths. Successful exploitation will lead to out-of-bounds memory reads that can expose sensitive process memory contents, or cause a crash of the packet dissection utility resulting in a denial of service condition.

This VLAN network device setup code contains a logical network configuration vulnerability caused by the incorrect memset operation that writes all zero values to the dev->broadcast field, overwriting the valid all-ones Ethernet broadcast address initialized by the preceding ether_setup call. The root cause is a developer error that replaces the standard required 6-byte FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF broadcast address with an all-zero value, breaking the interface’s ability to recognize and process incoming Ethernet broadcast frames. A remote adjacent network attacker can trigger this flaw by sending standard 802.1Q tagged broadcast traffic to the target system, which the misconfigured interface will silently discard instead of passing to upper network layers. Successful exploitation results in partial denial of service for all broadcast-reliant network services on the affected VLAN, preventing proper operation of protocols such as ARP, DHCP and local network service discovery.

This H.264 decoder parsing function contains a critical out-of-bounds write vulnerability affecting the reference index to POC mapping buffer. The root cause is that after incrementing the pui_map_ref_idx_to_poc_lx0 pointer by 1, the subsequent loop uses the attacker controlled ps_cur_slice->u1_num_ref_idx_lx_active[0] value as the upper bound for indexed writes to the offset pointer, with insufficient validation to ensure the accesses stay within the preallocated bounds of the underlying ppv_map_ref_idx_to_poc array. A remote attacker can trigger this issue by supplying a specially crafted malicious H.264 video bitstream that sets the num_ref_idx_lx_active value to a number larger than the maximum supported entry count for the mapping buffer. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to corrupt adjacent heap memory, leading to sensitive information disclosure, unexpected program crash or full remote code execution in the context of the decoder process.

This code contains a critical use-after-free vulnerability triggered by invalidation of the cache map iterator and underlying referenced cache entry following an unguarded erase operation. The root cause occurs when the first conditional block checking if cache_entry.IsDirty() and outgoing_file_map.count(resource_id) == 0 evaluates to true, as the call to cache_map->erase(cache_map_iter) deallocates the referenced CacheEntry instance and invalidates the cache_map_iter iterator, while the subsequent second conditional check still attempts to access the now freed cache_entry reference. An attacker who can manipulate the state of the target cache entry to meet the first conditional criteria can trigger this invalid memory access during the persistent file removal routine. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to unexpected program termination, arbitrary memory disclosure, or arbitrary code execution depending on the layout of adjacent heap memory holding related cache map structures.

This code contains an insufficient bounds validation vulnerability associated with the stack-allocated pm_results array used to store pattern matching derived protocol identification results. Successful exploitation will result in an immediate program crash and denial of service condition, and may allow unauthorized disclosure of sensitive host memory or arbitrary memory modification if the underlying driver logic performs unguarded read or write operations through the unvalidated pointers.

This C code contains an insufficient bounds checking vulnerability that leads to out of bounds memory read from the stack. The root cause is that after validating the total read length for UHID_OUTPUT events, the code directly passes the untrusted ev.u.output.size value provided by the uhid device to the btif_hh_setreport function without verifying that the value does not exceed the maximum size of the ev.u.output.data fixed length array. A local attacker with write access to the uhid character device can trigger this flaw by crafting a valid UHID_OUTPUT event with an ev.u.output.size value larger than the allocated size of the ev.u.output.data buffer. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to leak sensitive adjacent stack memory contents, including process memory addresses, authentication tokens or other sensitive runtime data, and can result in unexpected program crashes, privilege escalation or arbitrary code execution within the privileged Bluetooth system service.

This code contains a critical unconditioned stack-based out-of-bounds write vulnerability rooted in the lack of a guard to block execution of the null terminator write even when the length validation check fails. The fixed 16-byte stack-allocated buffer receives decoded data from mutt_b64_decode, and the returned len value is only checked for equality to sizeof clear minus 1 in a test macro that does not halt execution if the check fails, allowing a maliciously crafted encoded base64 input to produce a len value far larger than 15. This leads to out-of-bounds writes during the decode process and an additional out-of-bounds write of the null terminator past the end of the buffer, which can corrupt adjacent stack memory including stored return addresses and critical stack metadata. Successful exploitation of this flaw allows an attacker to achieve arbitrary code execution, leak sensitive in-memory credentials or cryptographic keys, or trigger a denial of service crash of the target process.

This code contains a critical use-after-free vulnerability rooted in insufficient reference count management for the passed nfs4_opendata calldata structure. The function performs multiple sequential accesses to fields of the data structure including data->cancelled, data->rpc_status, and data->o_res.rflags without holding a pre-incremented reference to the structure, allowing a concurrent execution path to call nfs4_opendata_put and free the backing memory mid-execution of this callback routine. An attacker who can induce a small timing window race condition between the asynchronous NFS RPC callback execution and a separate opendata release path can trigger dereferences of already freed heap memory. Successful exploitation of this flaw can lead to arbitrary kernel code execution, sensitive memory disclosure, or full system denial of service via uncontrolled memory corruption.

This code contains an unsigned integer wrap vulnerability that arises from the unvalidated left shift operation applied to the 8-bit png_byte bit_depth value. The root cause is the unguarded bitwise left shift of the bit_depth value followed by truncation to an 8-bit type, which performs the operation without checking that the shift result does not exceed the maximum value representable in a single byte, allowing the value to silently wrap to 0 when the pre-shift bit_depth is 128 or higher. An attacker who supplies a crafted malformed PNG file that sets the initial bit_depth to a value of 128 can trigger this wrap, which resets bit_depth to 0 and causes the function to re-execute its initial conditional block that sets colour_type to 0, creating an infinite non-terminating loop or producing completely unvalidated output values for colour_type, bit_depth, and palette_number. This can lead to denial of service via application hang or subsequent out of bounds memory read and write operations in downstream PNG decoding logic that consumes these unvalidated return parameters.

This code contains an insufficient input validation vulnerability for the mmap address randomization factor that undermines process address space safety. The root cause is that the value returned by arch_mmap_rnd() is used directly to calculate both mm->mmap_legacy_base and mm->mmap_base with no sanity checks to confirm the resulting mmap base address falls within the valid bounds of the architecture’s permitted userspace address range. A local attacker who can manipulate the output of arch_mmap_rnd() through a preceding bug or misconfiguration can trigger this flaw by supplying an overly large random_factor value that generates an mmap base address outside of allowed userspace limits. Successful exploitation can break address space layout randomization protections, cause unintended mappings to overlapping kernel memory regions, and enable the attacker to escalate privileges or leak sensitive kernel data from the running system.

This code contains a null pointer dereference vulnerability arising from missing validation of the dynamic allocation result returned by gf_isom_box_new when creating a fallback GF_DataReferenceBox instance. An attacker can trigger this issue by supplying a malformed ISO media file that omits the required dref box in the dinf container, while the target system is under low memory pressure that causes the gf_isom_box_new call to return NULL. Subsequent operations that access members of the unvalidated dref pointer will then attempt to read from or write to a null memory address, leading to unexpected program termination, denial of service, or in restricted memory scenarios arbitrary memory access and potential remote code execution.

This code contains a critical incomplete error handling vulnerability related to parsing of the MaxCrashReportsSize configuration value. The validation logic for the strtoul parsed value only logs an error message when the input is invalid, but does not assign a valid default value to the global g_settings_nMaxCrashReportsSize variable or halt processing, leaving the variable uninitialized if no prior valid value was set. A local attacker who supplies a maliciously crafted configuration file with a non-numeric, out-of-range, or empty MaxCrashReportsSize entry can reliably trigger this uninitialized variable state. When the uninitialized value is later used for crash report size limit calculations, memory allocation, or loop control operations, it leads to undefined behavior that can cause denial of service, out-of-bounds memory access, or arbitrary code execution with the full privileges of the running crash handling process.

This implementation contains a critical arbitrary command injection vulnerability, rooted in the complete lack of sanitization for all user-controllable string values inserted into the constructed command line. The code directly concatenates unvalidated values including method, manager->acl, manager->timeout, manager->user, manager->plugin, and manager->nameservers into the static cmd buffer via successive snprintf calls, with no escaping or filtering for shell metacharacters such as semicolons, ampersands, or backticks. A malicious actor who can supply specially crafted values for any of these controllable fields can break out of the intended command argument context to inject and execute arbitrary system commands when the returned command string is passed to a shell-based execution routine. Successful exploitation of this flaw grants the attacker full arbitrary code execution privileges matching those of the running process, allowing for complete compromise of the target host's data integrity, confidentiality, and operational availability.

This code contains an unvalidated input vulnerability that allows user-controlled parameter values to directly modify critical internal system state without any sanitization or bounds checking. The root cause is the lack of any validation logic applied to the values returned by the GET_PARAM macro before they are passed to the SetMode function or assigned to the set_cpu_used_ variable, meaning arbitrary attacker-supplied values are accepted as trusted valid input. An attacker can trigger this flaw by submitting maliciously crafted out-of-range or semantically invalid values for the two targeted parameters, such as an unrecognized mode identifier far outside the supported mode enumeration or an extremely large value for CPU usage that far exceeds the system’s predefined resource thresholds. Successful exploitation can result in unauthorized modification of operational mode, unexpected program control flow deviation, excessive CPU resource exhaustion, full denial of service, or even arbitrary code execution if the SetMode function processes untrusted mode values in an unsafe unvalidated manner.

This code contains a critical stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability rooted in missing bounds validation for the user-controlled input length value. The memcpy(outpkt.data, buffer, len) call directly copies untrusted input from the network-supplied buffer into the stack-allocated outpkt structure without verifying that the provided len parameter does not exceed the fixed preallocated size of the outpkt.data field. A remote unauthenticated attacker can trigger this flaw by sending a malicious TCP packet that sets the passed len argument to a value far larger than the maximum allowed size of the outpkt.data buffer. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to overwrite adjacent stack memory including critical control data such as function return pointers, leading to full remote code execution, unexpected program crash, or disclosure of sensitive in-memory data from the target VPN process.

This code contains an integer overflow vulnerability in the calculation of the allocation size passed to ArrayBuffer::createOrNull. The root cause is that the product of the two unsigned user-controllable parameters resizeWidth and resizeHeight is not validated for overflow before being passed as the first size argument to the allocation function, leading to a smaller than expected destination buffer being allocated when the product of the two values wraps around the maximum value for the underlying unsigned integer type. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying sufficiently large values for resizeWidth and resizeHeight that cause their arithmetic product to overflow to a small valid size that passes implicit allocation checks. When the subsequent SkPixmap is initialized with the full unclamped dimensions and correct row stride, the scalePixels operation will write pixel data far past the end of the undersized heap buffer, leading to out of bounds memory corruption that can enable arbitrary code execution or sensitive data leakage from adjacent heap memory regions.

This code contains multiple exploitable security vulnerabilities rooted in unsafe input validation and insecure temporary file handling. All input checks for non-NULL config, non-NULL filename, and non-empty filename are implemented using assert, which is fully compiled out and treated as a no-op in standard production builds that define the NDEBUG preprocessor macro, allowing an attacker to pass invalid NULL or empty string inputs that trigger unhandled undefined behavior such as crashes or arbitrary memory access. The temporary config file is created via fopen with no explicit permission restrictions, and the required restricted permission set is only applied after the file handle is opened, creating a time-of-check to time-of-use race window where a local unprivileged attacker can read or modify the partially written sensitive config data before the chmod call enforces user and group only access permissions. A successful attacker can achieve denial of service against the configuration service, exfiltrate sensitive configuration data such as stored credentials, or inject malicious configuration values that execute with the host process’s elevated system privileges.
There is no vulnerability.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds memory access vulnerability stemming from the incorrect order of conditional checks in the two for loops that iterate over image planes. The root cause is that the loop condition evaluates in->data[plane] before validating that plane is less than 4, so when plane increments to a value of 4, the code dereferences in->data[4] immediately without checking the plane index limit, reading outside the valid 0 to 3 index range of the AVFrame data pointer array. An attacker can trigger this issue by supplying a specially crafted video frame where the trailing bytes adjacent to the in->data array in memory hold a non-null value at the offset corresponding to index 4, causing the loop to execute with an out of bounds plane index value. This out of bounds access can propagate to the hblur and vblur functions, leading to subsequent out of bounds reads and writes across adjacent memory regions, which may result in sensitive information disclosure, unexpected application crashes, or even remote arbitrary code execution depending on the values retrieved from invalid memory addresses.

This H.264 slice parsing code contains an out-of-bounds memory write vulnerability originating from incomplete bounds validation of parsed reference index count values. The root cause is that the 32-bit unsigned values u4_temp and ui_temp1, populated via 1 + ih264d_uev calls for active reference indices, are only checked against a small 8-bit u1_max_ref_idx value that does not account for the full allocated size of the ppv_map_ref_idx_to_poc pointer array, allowing values far larger than the buffer's maximum supported index to proceed to subsequent processing. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a maliciously constructed H.264 bitstream that sets the num_ref_idx_l0_active_minus1 or num_ref_idx_l1_active_minus1 syntax elements to a large enough value to bypass the existing check, causing the following iterative index assignments to write past the allocated boundaries of the reference mapping buffer. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows the attacker to corrupt adjacent memory structures, leading to arbitrary code execution or sensitive data disclosure during the video decoding workflow.

This code contains an unvalidated bit offset manipulation vulnerability that leads to out-of-bounds memory read during VP9 stream information parsing. The root cause is that the code performs direct arithmetic modification of the vpx_read_bit_buffer bit_offset field via operations including rb.bit_offset += error_resilient ? 0 : 2 and rb.bit_offset += REF_FRAMES without verifying that the resulting offset value does not exceed the total number of bits available in the input data buffer. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a crafted malformed VP9 media stream with a non-keyframe header that meets all prior initial length checks, allowing the unvalidated offset increments to move the bit reader past the end of the allocated input buffer. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to unintended disclosure of sensitive adjacent memory content from the decoder process address space, or trigger an unhandled segmentation fault that crashes the decoder to produce a remote denial of service condition.

The primary security vulnerability in this function is a stack-based buffer overflow affecting the fixed 512-byte stack buffer bufferTmp. The root cause is that the meaningless tautology check if (&lp->filter) always evaluates to true as it inspects the non-NULL memory address of the lp->filter member rather than a valid filter existence flag, and the code never validates that the concatenated output of lp->filter.string and the dynamically built time filter string in buffer will fit within the 512 byte size of bufferTmp before calling snprintf. An attacker can supply a long, specially crafted timestring input that generates a very lengthy time filter clause to push the total output of the snprintf call well beyond the 512 byte buffer limit. This overflow corrupts adjacent stack memory including critical execution state and stored return addresses, allowing the attacker to achieve arbitrary remote code execution or trigger a critical denial of service condition that disrupts availability of the map hosting service.

The identified security vulnerability is an incorrect conditional logic flaw caused by unenforced operator precedence in the input bounds check for the GetBitContext structure. The root cause is the missing logical grouping of the OR clause within the conditional statement that checks gb->size_in_bits == 8 and ctx divx version or xvid build values, which evaluates such that the size_in_bits == 8 check is entirely skipped when the codec tag matches QMP4, allowing the decoder to process undersized bit buffers without returning the expected invalid data error. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a malicious MPEG4 media file with the QMP4 codec tag and a bit buffer smaller than 8 bits, causing the decoder to read out of bounds from adjacent heap memory regions during startcode parsing. This out of bounds read can expose sensitive process memory contents to the attacker, induce a crash leading to denial of service, or in unfavorable memory layouts corrupt internal decoder state to enable arbitrary code execution.

This code contains a critical unvalidated null pointer dereference vulnerability that occurs when the GetWebsiteSetting function returns an empty null std::unique_ptr for the requested origin and embedding origin pair. The root cause is the missing validation step for the returned setting variable before the code invokes setting->Remove directly, with no check to confirm the smart pointer holds a valid non-null underlying pointer before member access. A remote attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying carefully constructed origin values that cause the underlying website settings storage layer to return no valid stored setting entry, forcing the code to attempt memory access through a null pointer. This will immediately cause a hard process crash that enables a reliable denial of service attack against the host application, and under favorable memory layout conditions may even allow an attacker to execute arbitrary malicious code within the context of the running browser process.

The primary security vulnerability in the provided function is insufficient bounds checking that enables out-of-bounds access to shared memory and adjacent process memory. The root cause is that the code directly assigns the unvalidated shm_offset value to the mem_params structure, and never validates that the sum of shm_offset and sizeof QuerySync does not exceed the total size of the returned shared memory buffer referenced by buffer.size. A malicious attacker can provide a carefully constructed large shm_offset value that positions the target QuerySync operation outside the legitimate bounds of the allocated shared memory segment. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to trigger unauthorized reads or writes to arbitrary adjacent memory regions in the privileged decoder process, leading to sensitive credential disclosure, heap memory corruption, or arbitrary code execution that fully compromises the graphics service runtime.

This code contains a time-of-check to time-of-use origin validation bypass vulnerability that allows attackers to circumvent intended same-origin restrictions for the extension guest view. The root cause is that the security logic checking that the target URL is either equal to url::kAboutBlankURL or shares the same origin as extension_url_ runs against the unmodified input url, prior to the call to FilterURL which is permitted to alter the url variable in place to a completely different value. An attacker who can influence the behavior of FilterURL to rewrite the url to an arbitrary cross-origin destination after the initial validation step will evade all prior access controls, as no re-check of the URL origin is performed after the FilterURL mutation. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to load untrusted attacker-controlled content directly in the privileged extension guest process, leading to sensitive data exfiltration, arbitrary script execution with extension permissions, and full compromise of the browser extension's security boundary.

This code contains a critical object lifetime management use-after-free vulnerability rooted in improper ordering of reference counting operations in the class member function. The Release() call is intended to decrement the reference count of the hosting ExtensionTtsSpeakFunction instance, and will immediately deallocate the entire object once the reference count drops to zero, leaving no valid backing memory for the instance after the call completes. Since the member function is still executing after Release() returns, the implicit function epilogue operations that access the hidden this pointer to restore execution state will operate on freed, potentially reallocated memory, leading to undefined behavior. An attacker who can manipulate the reference count of the target instance to trigger premature deallocation during this function’s execution can exploit this issue to corrupt heap memory, induce a denial of service, or achieve remote arbitrary code execution within the context of the hosting process.

This code contains multiple unmitigated stack-based buffer overflow vulnerabilities stemming from unsafe use of the sprintf function on fixed-size stack-allocated character arrays. The root cause is that sprintf performs no bounds checking on input data, and the user-controlled test_path parameter can be supplied with an arbitrarily long value that exceeds the 1024-byte size of the filename buffer when combined with the appended "input" or "env" suffix during path construction. An attacker can trigger this overflow by passing a specially crafted overly long test_path value that writes past the end of the filename array, and a second independent overflow can be triggered if the JSON error text stored in error.text is sufficiently long to exceed the 1024-byte errstr buffer during the subsequent error reporting sprintf call. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities allows an attacker to corrupt adjacent stack memory, overwrite critical execution state such as function return addresses, and achieve arbitrary code execution or leak sensitive internal process data.
There is no vulnerability.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds memory read vulnerability when processing PNG images with palette color type. The root cause is that the code assigns the value returned by the sample function directly to this->palette_index, then uses that unvalidated unsigned integer value as an index into the palette array when colour_type equals 3, with no check to confirm the index falls within the valid bounds of the allocated palette buffer. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a specially crafted malicious PNG file that stores a palette index value far larger than the actual number of entries in the embedded palette structure. Successful exploitation of this flaw allows the attacker to read arbitrary adjacent memory regions, expose sensitive runtime data from the process address space, cause unexpected program termination, or potentially execute arbitrary code if the unvalidated palette color values are later used in downstream unsafe memory operations.

This CUT image parsing implementation contains an unvalidated path traversal vulnerability in its palette file loading logic. The root cause is that the code derives the palette file path by modifying the original input image filename without enforcing strict sanitization or restricting output paths to the intended working directory, and when no valid dot separator is found in the filename, it truncates the full input path to the parent directory then attempts to open a file directly from that unregulated location. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a specially crafted input filename that contains no dot character and ends in a path separator such as / or \, which forces the parser to skip appending the .PAL or .pal suffix and instead attempt to open a user-specified arbitrary local file as the palette source. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to read the full contents of arbitrary files on the target host filesystem, resulting in sensitive information disclosure that may expose private credentials, cryptographic keys, or other restricted system data.

This code contains an unvalidated user-controlled segment count vulnerability that arises from directly assigning kiocb->ki_nr_segs to the raw, user-provided kiocb->ki_nbytes value before any bounds checking on the number of scatter-gather segments is performed. The root cause is that rw_copy_check_uvector treats its third integer argument as the total number of user-supplied iovec structures, but the code passes the user-controlled kiocb->ki_nbytes as this segment count value, then later overwrites kiocb->ki_nbytes to store the total aggregated transfer byte count returned by the function, leaving the unvalidated original user input stored in kiocb->ki_nr_segs. A local attacker can submit an asynchronous IO request with an excessively large value set for the kiocb->ki_nbytes field, bypassing intended kernel limits on the maximum number of allowed vectored IO segments. This leads to out-of-bounds memory access when the kernel later iterates over the allocated iovec array using the unvalidated large segment count, enabling arbitrary kernel memory disclosure, corruption, and full local privilege escalation to root.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds memory access vulnerability stemming from a complete lack of input validation for the begin_index and end_index parameters passed to the CopyCachedSubsequence function. The root cause is that the function directly uses these unvalidated size_t values to index into the current paint artifact's display item list and iterate over the range defined by the two parameters, with no checks to ensure begin_index does not exceed end_index or that end_index stays within the valid bounds of the existing display item list. An attacker who can supply manipulated values for these two parameters can trigger out-of-bounds reads from adjacent arbitrary memory regions, or trigger invalid memory access that crashes the browser rendering process. This flaw can lead to sensitive memory disclosure that breaks renderer process isolation, or enable further arbitrary code execution in the high privilege rendering context if paired with additional targeted memory manipulation primitives.

The identified security vulnerability is insufficient validation of user-provided embedded pointer values in the qib character device write handling routine. This flaw occurs because the code directly casts unsigned long values retrieved from user input in fields such as spu_base_info, ctxt_info, and sdma_inflight to user space pointers, without performing any checks to confirm the referenced memory ranges are within valid, user-accessible address bounds. A local attacker can trigger this vulnerability by sending a crafted write request to the exposed qib device file, supplying malicious pointer and size values that reference out of bounds or kernel-side memory addresses. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to leak sensitive kernel memory contents, trigger unintended out of bounds memory access, achieve local privilege escalation, or crash the underlying system to cause a permanent denial of service.

This code contains an unvalidated unfiltered input propagation vulnerability that can lead to unintended sensitive data disclosure and cross-extension privilege escalation. The root cause is that the function directly appends the unvalidated changed_properties DictionaryValue to the broadcast event argument list without implementing any access control checks or data sanitization to restrict the fields included in the broadcasted event payload. A malicious local process or compromised browser subcomponent that can supply a crafted DictionaryValue containing restricted internal tab metadata can trigger this code path to broadcast sensitive non-public tab state to all untrusted extensions subscribed to the onTabUpdated event. Successful exploitation can expose private user data including hidden tab URLs, partial form input, or incognito session identifiers to unvetted third-party extensions, violating core browser security isolation guarantees for extension event data.

This parse_index function contains an unvalidated untrusted integer vulnerability tied to the entry_count field extracted directly from the untrusted input index header. The root cause is that the code reads the entry_count value from the untrusted header structure without performing any sanity checks to confirm the value is consistent with the total remaining valid buffer capacity before passing it to the git_idxmap_resize or git_idxmap_icase_resize memory allocation routines. An attacker can trigger this flaw by providing a specially crafted malicious git index file that sets the entry_count header field to an extremely large or malformed value that far exceeds the number of entries that can fit within the provided input buffer, even when the full content of the malicious file passes the initial checksum validation. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to trigger excessive memory consumption that leads to a severe denial of service condition, or cause an integer overflow during the resize operation that results in subsequent heap memory corruption and arbitrary code execution on the target system.

This code contains an integer truncation vulnerability related to the handling of the literal_index counter. The root cause is that literal_index is declared as a 32-bit unsigned integer, but it is directly cast to a 16-bit unsigned type when assigned to context_p->lit_object.index, with no explicit check to confirm the value of literal_index does not exceed the maximum value of a 16-bit unsigned integer before the cast. An attacker can trigger this issue by feeding the parser a specially crafted input that generates more than 65535 unique literals before the literal pool size limit is enforced, causing the 32-bit literal_index value to wrap around when truncated to 16 bits. This incorrect wrapped index value will cause the parser to reference unintended and potentially out-of-bounds entries in the literal pool, leading to corrupted memory access, unexpected program behavior, and possible arbitrary code execution or full runtime compromise.

This H.264 decoder function contains an unvalidated offset calculation vulnerability that leads to out-of-bounds memory read access during error slice skip processing. The root cause is the missing bounds check for the value of ps_dec->u4_num_mbs_prev_nmb when u1_num_mbs is 0 and ps_dec->u1_separate_parse is 0, which causes the code to compute the pointer ps_cur_mb_info as ps_dec->ps_nmb_info plus ps_dec->u4_num_mbs_prev_nmb minus 1 without verifying the resulting offset falls within the allocated bounds of the ps_nmb_info buffer. An attacker can trigger this condition by supplying a maliciously crafted H.264 video stream that sets the current macroblock count to zero and initializes the previous macroblock count value to zero or a very large unvalidated integer during corrupted slice error handling routines. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to unintended disclosure of adjacent heap or stack memory contents, crash the vulnerable media decoding process, or in worst case scenarios allow arbitrary code execution within the security context of the running decoder process.

This IDE DMA emulation code for a system hypervisor contains a critical insufficient bounds checking vulnerability stemming from a misplaced preprocessor directive that breaks validation of DMA transfer parameters. The root cause is a stray #endif placed immediately after the debug printf statement that cuts off execution of required parameter update logic for the current DMA transfer chunk, meaning the subsequent ide_sect_range_ok routine validates stale sector number and sector count values rather than the actual parameters for the pending new IO operation. A malicious guest actor can trigger this flaw by sending a specially crafted multi-sector IDE DMA command to the emulated storage device, which causes the code to skip all range checks for the newly calculated transfer window. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to initiate unvalidated out-of-bounds read, write or trim operations against the underlying host block device, leading to sensitive system data leakage, persistent host storage corruption and full arbitrary code execution on the host virtualization layer.

This code contains a critical unvalidated pointer access vulnerability originating from the use of debug-only DCHECK macros to verify that the profile pointer and profile->GetPrefs() return non-null values, as these assertion checks are completely removed in production release builds leaving no runtime validation of the pointer values. An attacker that can trigger execution of this function with a null or uninitialized profile pointer in a production build will cause the application to attempt to dereference the invalid pointer when calling profile->GetPrefs() during the DataReductionProxyIOData initialization sequence. Successful exploitation of this flaw results in an unhandled process crash that delivers a permanent denial of service for the affected browser instance, and under favorable memory layout conditions may allow an attacker to corrupt adjacent heap memory to escalate privileges or execute arbitrary malicious code.

This code contains an unhandled cleanup gap vulnerability for the primary account signout flow when the AccountConsistencyMethod value is not set to kDice. The root cause is the unconditional continue statement executed in the else branch of the nested account_consistency_ check, which skips the subsequent token fetcher cleanup loop entirely for the signed out primary account, leaving active pending token fetcher entries associated with the signed out account in memory. An attacker who can trigger a signout flow for the primary account under a non kDice account consistency configuration can leave stale unprocessed token fetchers active in the background. This can lead to unauthorized ongoing operations for a fully signed out user account, unintended exposure of leftover user authentication state, and potential memory safety issues if the underlying account data is freed while the orphaned token fetchers still hold active references to it.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds read vulnerability stemming from unvalidated array indexing of the kwset->delta buffer referenced by d1. An unprivileged local attacker can invoke the bind syscall on an L2TP IPv6 socket with a specially crafted, extremely short sockaddr buffer and corresponding small addr_len value to force the kernel to read unintended adjacent kernel memory beyond the bounds of the provided user buffer. This leak of sensitive adjacent kernel memory can expose restricted system state, address layout information, or credential data that can be further abused to escalate privileges or bypass kernel memory protection mechanisms.
