A remote unauthenticated attacker can trigger this condition by sending a specially crafted MINISSDPD_SUBMIT request that passes initial validation steps but fails the later length or forbidden character checks for the usn field. Repeated exploitation of this vulnerability will exhaust the target process's available heap memory, leading to denial of service via process out of memory termination or unresponsiveness to all legitimate incoming requests.

This C code contains a potential unvalidated out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the TCP SYNACK generation path for IPv6 connections. The root cause occurs when the code checks that the ireq->pktopts pointer is non-NULL to retrieve the original flow label, but performs no validation to confirm the referenced skb object has enough allocated data space to safely access the full IPv6 header via ipv6_hdr, leaving the access unguarded against truncated or corrupted stored packets. An attacker can trigger this flaw by sending a malformed truncated IPv6 SYN packet that the system partially accepts, resulting in a stored pktopts skb whose data buffer is too small to contain a complete IPv6 header. Successful exploitation can leak sensitive arbitrary kernel memory contents into the outgoing SYNACK packet to expose internal system data, or trigger an unrecoverable kernel panic that causes a full system denial of service.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds read vulnerability stemming from incorrect bounds calculation for the loop indexing of the cast Type pointer. The root cause is that the loop uses the raw byte length of the input audio_data buffer as the maximum index value for the output Type array, when the maximum valid number of Type elements that can safely fit in the byte buffer is the total byte length divided by the size of a single Type object. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by providing any length value that is not an exact multiple of the size of one Type element, or a length value larger than the actual size of the underlying allocation pointed to by audio_data, to force the loop to read memory well past the end of the valid audio_data region. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows an attacker to leak arbitrary adjacent memory contents from the stack or heap, potentially exposing sensitive data such as encryption keys, user credentials, or internal process state that can be used to further compromise the target system.

This code contains an unvalidated return value vulnerability in the Content-Language HTTP header parsing logic. The root cause is that the code calls header_content_language.find(',') and passes the resulting comma_index directly to the Truncate method without verifying that a comma was actually located, as the find operation returns the special npos sentinel value when no comma exists, which is a maximum size_t value far larger than the actual length of the header string. A remote attacker can trigger this flaw by serving a crafted HTTP response that includes a Content-Language header value with no comma characters, causing the truncate operation to execute with an invalid index. This can lead to unexpected undefined behavior including out-of-bounds memory access, incorrect sanitization of the document content language state, or corruption of adjacent string values stored in the same memory heap, potentially allowing the attacker to bypass intended web security controls or execute arbitrary malicious code in the context of the hosting browser renderer process.

This code contains an integer underflow vulnerability in the calculation of the inline_bytes variable, which originates from the lack of validation that the sum of bytes subtracted from the original rqstp->rq_res.len value does not exceed the original total length. An attacker can craft a malicious RDMA RPC request with oversized write and reply chunk arrays that cause the ret values returned from send_write_chunks and send_reply_chunks to be large enough to reduce inline_bytes to a negative value. When this negative signed integer is passed to downstream functions that treat it as an unsigned size parameter, it can trigger out-of-bounds memory reads across adjacent kernel memory pages during response transmission. This flaw can allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to leak sensitive kernel data, corrupt adjacent page or kernel memory metadata, and ultimately achieve arbitrary code execution in the privileged kernel context.

The identified security vulnerability is an unchecked malloc return value that leads to a critical NULL pointer dereference risk. The root cause is that the code does not validate that the requested heap allocation for the new downmix_module_t structure succeeded before directly accessing structure members, immediately executing module->itfe = &gDownmixInterface after the malloc call without any prior null check. An attacker can trigger this flaw by exhausting available system memory to force the malloc call to return NULL during a valid call to DownmixLib_Create for a registered effect UUID. Successful exploitation will cause an immediate process crash resulting in a denial of service for the audio effect processing pipeline, and may enable arbitrary memory corruption if an attacker can control the memory returned from a failed malloc implementation under specific low memory conditions.

This C code contains a critical out-of-bounds read and subsequent heap buffer overflow vulnerability rooted in the absence of validation for the source character pointer retrieved via the this->*str dereference. The root cause is that the code passes the unchecked src pointer directly to strlen without confirming that src points to a properly null-terminated C string within valid, bounded process memory. An attacker who can manipulate the src pointer value to point to a non-null-terminated buffer can trigger strlen to sequentially read past the end of the allocated memory region until it encounters a null byte, which may produce a length value of SIZE_MAX such that the subsequent len + 1 calculation wraps around to zero. This leads to the allocation of a zero-sized heap buffer that is too small to hold the full data referenced by the unbounded strlen result, causing strcpy to write well past the end of the destination heap allocation, enabling full arbitrary remote code execution or sensitive memory disclosure of values such as cryptographic keys or stack canaries stored in adjacent process address space.

This C code contains multiple distinct security and reliability vulnerabilities that impact the stability and expected operation of the embedded web server. The first root cause is the complete lack of NULL checks on all values returned from strdup, which allows an out of memory condition to trigger unhandled NULL pointer dereferences when the code later accesses the copied strings for the WWW directory path or log file paths, resulting in an immediate service crash. A second critical flaw is the incorrect conditional check for freeing the default log_file allocation, which compares the heap pointer returned by strdup to the memory address of the static DEFAULT_LOG_FILE string literal, ensuring the heap allocated default log_file buffer is never freed and leading to permanent memory leaks that can be exploited for denial of service via repeated process restarts. The code also performs no bounds validation on the port value returned by atoi, allowing a malicious local attacker to pass a negative or out of range port number that causes unexpected binding behavior or unhandled failures during daemon initialization.
There is no vulnerability.

This code contains an unvalidated integer overflow vulnerability in the regset data size calculation step that occurs before kernel memory allocation. The root cause is the lack of bounds checking on the product of regset->n and regset->size when computing the size variable, allowing the multiplication of two size_t values to wrap around the maximum size limit for the type and produce a smaller than intended allocation size passed to kmalloc. A local attacker with the ability to provide a malformed user regset view can trigger this overflow to allocate a small kernel buffer, then cause the regset->get routine to write a far larger volume of regset data past the end of the allocated heap buffer. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows the attacker to corrupt adjacent kernel heap memory, escalate execution privileges to root, leak sensitive kernel memory contents, or trigger a complete system crash and denial of service.

This Vp9Parser constructor that only invokes the Reset() method contains a potential uninitialized memory vulnerability if the referenced Reset() routine does not explicitly initialize every internal member variable of the Vp9Parser class. The root cause is that the constructor provides no validation or guarantee that all class fields are set to valid, defined values before any other class methods are invoked, leaving uninitialized values in memory regions associated with the instantiated class object. An attacker can trigger this flaw by submitting malformed VP9 media content that triggers execution paths in later parser functions that read the uninitialized member variables before they are assigned proper values. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to arbitrary out of bounds memory read or write operations, unexpected program crashes, or even full remote arbitrary code execution depending on how the uninitialized values are processed in downstream parsing logic.

This code contains a critical dangling pointer vulnerability in the PHP nested unserialization processing logic. The root cause is that the function inserts the stack-local uninitialized zval d directly into the target HashTable before it is fully populated by the subsequent call to php_var_unserialize_internal, and if that nested unserialization call returns an error, the function exits early without removing the stack-allocated zval from the HashTable, leaving the HashTable referencing memory that resides on the current function's stack frame. An attacker can trigger this condition by supplying a specially crafted malicious serialized payload that causes the inner unserialization step to fail mid-execution, resulting in the HashTable holding a stale pointer that will be overwritten by values from subsequent function calls to the same stack location. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows an attacker to achieve arbitrary memory read and write primitives, leading to full remote code execution on the target PHP runtime environment.

This code contains a critical undefined behavior vulnerability affecting OS_CHROMEOS builds that use a debug-only CHECK macro that is stripped and marked as unreachable in release configurations. The root cause is that the OS_CHROMEOS code path executes only a CHECK(false) statement followed by an explicit return NULL, and compiler optimization will eliminate the subsequent return NULL statement entirely if the CHECK macro is marked as unreachable, leaving the function with no valid return path for that execution branch. When an attacker triggers a call to the Create function on an affected optimized OS_CHROMEOS build, execution will flow past the unreachable marker without populating a valid return value, resulting in an uninitialized stack pointer being returned to the caller. Subsequent dereferencing of this uninitialized pointer by downstream application code can lead to unexpected memory access, arbitrary control flow hijacking, and full remote code execution with the full privileges of the running browser process.

This C code contains a critical null pointer dereference vulnerability in the V8 JavaScript binding implementation of the DirectoryEntry getDirectory DOM API. The root cause is that the local flags RefPtr variable is only assigned a valid WebKitFlags instance if the second input argument is both non-null non-undefined and a V8 object, leaving flags holding a null pointer if the second argument is a non-null non-undefined primitive value such as a string, number or boolean. A remote attacker can reliably trigger this vulnerability by calling the exposed JavaScript getDirectory function with a valid path value and a non-object primitive as the second flags parameter, which skips the flags initialization block while proceeding to invoke the four-argument overload of imp->getDirectory that expects a valid non-null flags pointer. Successful exploitation of this flaw will result in an unexpected renderer process crash leading to denial of service, and may allow for arbitrary code execution if the null pointer offset leads to writable or executable memory access under attacker control.

This code contains a critical unvalidated input vulnerability leading to LDAP filter injection during the LDAP authentication check flow. The root cause is that the code only rejects usernames containing the characters "*()" and does not perform full proper escaping or block all reserved LDAP filter metacharacters that can modify the structure of the dynamically constructed search query. A remote unauthenticated attacker can trigger this flaw by submitting a specially crafted username with embedded filter control sequences that alter the LDAP search logic to return a valid user entry even for non-existent or unauthorized accounts. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to fully bypass the intended password-based LDAP authentication flow, gaining unauthorized access to all protected web resources behind the Cherokee web server's access control layer.

This code contains an unsafe unchecked downcasting vulnerability that stems from the use of a raw static_cast to convert the generic EntrySync pointer returned by helper->getResult to a DirectoryEntrySync pointer with no prior validation that the returned object is actually of the expected directory entry type. An attacker who can manipulate the underlying file system operation to return a non-directory entry such as a regular file entry can trigger this flaw by providing a path that resolves to a non-directory resource to the getDirectory method. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability leads to invalid type confusion memory access, where operations intended for a DirectoryEntrySync object are performed on an incompatible object layout, enabling out of bounds memory access and corruption that can lead to remote code execution or sensitive information disclosure within the context of the hosting application process.

This code contains an unvalidated input file descriptor vulnerability that occurs because the CameraDeviceClient::dump function accepts an unvetted fd parameter and passes it directly to the mFrameProcessor->dump call and subsequent dumpDevice call without performing any validation of the descriptor state or access permissions. An attacker with the ability to invoke this exposed privileged interface can supply a maliciously chosen file descriptor that references a sensitive system file, protected process memory region, or restricted kernel device to force the camera service to write its internal state data to the attacker specified target. Successful exploitation leads to unauthorized disclosure of sensitive camera identifiers, client process IDs, and internal operational state, and may even allow modification of critical system resources if the supplied file descriptor points to a writable privileged location.

This code contains a critical out-of-bounds write memory corruption vulnerability stemming from insufficient buffer size calculation for the temporary split buffer. The root cause is that the bufsize value used to size both the stack-allocated splitbuf and the dynamically allocated buf is derived exclusively from the numrows parameter via JPC_CEILDIVPOW2(numrows, 1), with no consideration of the numcols parameter that controls how many jpc_fix_t elements are copied per row into the buffer. An attacker can trigger this flaw by providing crafted malformed image data that sets a very large value for numcols, which causes the nested per-row copy loops to write far more elements than the allocated buffer can hold, overflowing past the edge of the stack or heap memory assigned to the buffer. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows an attacker to corrupt adjacent in-process memory, execute arbitrary code in the context of the running application, or trigger a crash that results in a denial of service condition.

The primary security vulnerability in this restartable deterministic ECDSA signing function is missing explicit secure zeroization of the stack-allocated data buffer that holds sensitive private key material during the HMAC_DRBG seeding process. The root cause is that the data array is populated with the raw binary private key d and the computed message hash value, but no secure memory erasure routine is applied to the buffer after the HMAC_DRBG instance is initialized, leaving the sensitive values resident in process stack memory after the function completes execution. An attacker with the ability to perform even limited residual stack memory disclosure from the same process address space can extract fragments of the ECDSA private key, which can be combined with partial signature data to fully reconstruct the full private key value. This flaw can be triggered by invoking the function with a valid restart context and interrupting the signing flow mid execution, then running a secondary operation that reads uninitialized stack regions to retrieve the leftover private key bytes, enabling full malicious signature forgery for arbitrary messages.

This code contains an integer underflow vulnerability in the calculation of the socket buffer gso_size value for IPv6 UFO fragmented packets. The root cause is that the arithmetic operation mtu - fragheaderlen - sizeof(struct frag_hdr) performs no validation to confirm the mtu value is larger than the combined sum of the two subtracted values, allowing the intermediate result to wrap around to a very large positive unsigned integer if a small attacker-controlled mtu value is provided. A local or remote attacker can trigger this underflow by specifying a crafted mtu value smaller than the sum of the IPv6 fragment header length and the frag header size during large UDP packet transmission, leading to an invalid excessively large gso_size being stored in the socket buffer shared info. This invalid gso_size will cause subsequent network stack processing logic to write far beyond the allocated bounds of the socket buffer, resulting in kernel memory corruption, arbitrary code execution in kernel context, or full system compromise.

This code contains a critical use-after-free vulnerability in the HTMLMediaElement network state transition routine. The root cause stems from the fact that the call to ScheduleEvent for the progress event can execute registered JavaScript event handler code synchronously during browser event dispatch, which may release all references to the parent HTMLMediaElement object and deallocate its underlying memory before subsequent operations run. An attacker can trigger this flaw by hosting a media element on a malicious web page and registering a custom progress event handler that explicitly removes the media element from the DOM and drops all remaining references to the object during event execution. Successful exploitation lets the attacker access and modify already freed heap memory when the code later invokes SetNetworkState on the deallocated instance, leading to arbitrary code execution or a destabilizing denial of service from corrupt heap state.

This code contains an unvalidated pointer access vulnerability that leads to a potential null pointer dereference during object construction. The root cause is that the member initializer sequence calls web_contents->GetMainFrame()->GetProcess() without checking that the pointer returned by GetMainFrame is non-null, which can occur if the referenced WebContents instance has not fully initialized its main frame at the time the HeadlessWebContentsImpl constructor runs. A remote or local attacker who can trigger instantiation of this HeadlessWebContentsImpl object at an early lifecycle stage before the main frame is fully populated can reliably trigger this flaw. Successful exploitation will result in a critical browser process crash and associated denial of service, and in edge cases with controlled memory layout, may allow an attacker to execute arbitrary malicious code within the privileged browser process context.

This code contains an insufficient input validation vulnerability for USB interface descriptor values that can lead to stack-based out-of-bounds memory access. The root cause is that the code only emits a warning when the parsed interface number inum is greater than or equal to the declared total number of interfaces nintf_orig, and does not enforce that all inum values are bounded by USB_MAXINTERFACES before they are used to index the stack-allocated inums and nalts arrays. This vulnerability can be triggered by a physically local attacker that supplies a malicious USB device crafted with a malformed configuration descriptor holding interface descriptors with arbitrarily large bInterfaceNumber fields. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to corrupt adjacent kernel stack memory, leading to privilege escalation, arbitrary kernel code execution, and full compromise of the host system.

This vulnerability is an unhandled integer division by zero flaw in the gdAlphaBlend alpha blending color calculation logic. The root cause is that the code does not validate that the extracted src_alpha and dst_alpha values fall within the expected non-negative range bounded by gdAlphaTransparent, and only handles exact edge cases for fully opaque or fully transparent alpha values, allowing the derived src_weight and dst_weight values to sum to zero. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying specially crafted src and dst truecolor input values with alpha components outside the expected valid range, such that the arithmetic operations produce a tot_weight value of zero before the red, green, and blue color channel calculations execute. Successful exploitation will result in an unexpected program crash due to the division by zero fault, leading to denial of service for any application that calls this function with untrusted input, and may enable arbitrary code execution in memory-constrained or unprotected runtime environments.

This code contains an unvalidated offset-based out-of-bounds kernel memory write vulnerability. The root cause is that the else branch under the initial addr check performs pointer arithmetic using the fully unvalidated user-controlled addr value, with no checks to ensure the resulting destination pointer remains within the bounds of the associated struct pt_regs memory region. A local attacker can supply a specially crafted small positive addr value that passes the initial bounds check against the dummy32 struct offset, allowing them to write arbitrary 32-bit values to unintended kernel addresses offset from the valid regs pointer. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to corrupt sensitive adjacent kernel task state, modify execution control flow, and escalate local privileges to unrestricted root access on the target system.

This code contains a critical heap buffer overflow vulnerability stemming from the unsafe use of the strftime function with a fully user-controlled format string. The root cause is that the function takes an untrusted user-supplied mask input, processes it through a series of string replacement operations that do not restrict or sanitize percent characters used for strftime format specifiers, then passes the resulting mask_decoded4 value directly as the format argument to strftime, with a destination buffer allocated as strlen(mask_decoded4) plus only 256 extra bytes to hold expanded date values. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a crafted mask containing a large number of strftime format specifiers that expand to far more than 256 bytes of output, causing strftime to write past the end of the heap-allocated mask_decoded5 buffer. Successful exploitation allows an attacker to corrupt adjacent heap memory, leak sensitive stack or heap contents, and ultimately achieve arbitrary code execution within the Weechat process context.

This C code contains a critical integer overflow vulnerability in the SUN image format parsing logic. The root cause is that the code only validates overflow for the product of sun_info.height and sun_info.width, but does not extend this overflow check to account for the additional bytes required to store pixel data at non 8-bit depths, allowing the calculated total pixel buffer size to wrap around to a small value that passes subsequent memory allocation sanity checks. This flaw can be triggered when an attacker provides a maliciously crafted SUN image file with carefully chosen large width, height, and depth values that produce an undercounted total pixel size after arithmetic overflow. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to read excessive amounts of pixel data past the end of a small allocated heap buffer, leading to out of bounds memory access, sensitive information disclosure, or even arbitrary remote code execution on the vulnerable host.

This code contains an improper memory write vulnerability stemming from an incorrect size argument passed to yr_arena_write_data. The root cause is that the code passes sizeof(string) as the write length, where string is a local YR_STRING pointer, so the value evaluates to the size of the pointer type rather than the size of the underlying YR_STRING structure, leading to only 4 or 8 bytes of stack data holding the pointer value being written to the destination arena instead of the full expected YR_STRING object. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a crafted malformed input file that generates a non-chained string match where the target string's matches count is zero, forcing execution flow to the faulty write call. This corrupted arena state can then be leveraged by an attacker to execute out of bounds memory reads and writes, leading to arbitrary code execution or unexpected crash and denial of service of the affected YARA scanning process.

This userns_install function contains a critical null pointer dereference vulnerability that arises from unvalidated access to the current task’s mm struct. The root cause is that the code executes the check atomic_read(&current->mm->mm_users) > 1 without first verifying that current->mm is not NULL, an assumption that fails for kernel threads which do not possess a user address space and set their mm pointer to null. An attacker can trigger this flaw by manipulating execution flow to invoke the function on a kernel task with no attached user memory management structure, causing the kernel to attempt a memory read at an invalid low address offset from zero. This attack will immediately trigger a fatal kernel page fault that results in a complete system denial of service, and in optimized exploitation scenarios may allow an adversary to corrupt adjacent kernel memory and achieve full privilege escalation to execute arbitrary code at privileged kernel level.

This code contains a critical type confusion vulnerability stemming from the unvalidated casting of a user or externally controlled void pointer parameter directly to a strongly typed InputMethodLibraryImpl pointer. The root cause is the complete lack of validation that the supplied void pointer actually points to a valid, properly initialized InputMethodLibraryImpl instance, as the only pre-cast check verifies execution is on the UI thread and does not perform any pointer safety or type matching checks. A remote or local attacker can trigger this vulnerability by passing a carefully crafted invalid pointer value as the object argument that points to arbitrary attacker-controlled memory, which will then be treated as a valid InputMethodLibraryImpl instance when the UpdateProperty method is invoked. Successful exploitation of this flaw can allow the attacker to read unintended sensitive memory regions, corrupt adjacent heap or stack memory, and ultimately achieve arbitrary code execution in the context of the running browser process.

This code contains a critical unreachable code vulnerability caused by an unconditional goto Exit statement placed immediately after assigning the local bitmap->width value, which skips all subsequent bitmap allocation, rasterization, and pixel processing logic entirely. The root cause is a misplaced jump instruction that prevents proper initialization of the bitmap buffer pointer and validation of the calculated width and height dimensions, leaving the bitmap structure with valid-looking dimension values but a stale or uninitialized buffer pointer. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a specially crafted font file that produces a valid outline cbox and passes the initial format and render mode checks to reach the misplaced goto statement. When downstream code attempts to read or write pixel data through the uninitialized bitmap buffer pointer, it can access arbitrary memory regions, leading to out of bounds memory corruption, sensitive information leakage, or even remote arbitrary code execution depending on the surrounding memory layout.

This code contains two distinct security flaws rooted in missing runtime input validation and unsafe pointer dereferencing. First, the page_number value is only validated via the debug-only DCHECK_GE macro, which is stripped from all release builds, leaving no active check to prevent negative, excessively large, or otherwise invalid page number values from being processed at runtime. Second, the function directly dereferences the print_pages_params_ pointer to retrieve the preview_request_id value without any prior null check, creating an unguarded memory access path that can trigger an invalid read if the pointer is uninitialized or set to null. A remote or local attacker that can supply controlled inputs to this function can trigger these unvalidated conditions to cause a critical process crash resulting in denial of service, or potentially leak sensitive in-process memory contents depending on the specific memory layout surrounding the invalid pointer access.

This code contains an unsigned integer underflow vulnerability that leads to a critical heap-based buffer overflow during USB HID transfer data copying. The root cause occurs when the code executes corrected_size-- after confirming transfer_priv->hid_buffer[0] == 0, with no prior validation that the current value of corrected_size is greater than zero. If an attacker configures a zero value for transfer_priv->hid_expected_size and ensures the first byte of the HID buffer is set to 0, the unsigned 32-bit corrected_size variable will underflow to the maximum 32-bit unsigned value, causing the subsequent memcpy operation to copy far more bytes than the allocated size of the hid_dest destination buffer. Successful exploitation of this flaw allows an attacker to corrupt adjacent heap memory, execute arbitrary code, or trigger a severe denial of service crash of the vulnerable process handling malicious USB HID device traffic.
There is no vulnerability.

This code contains a global shared state denial of service vulnerability rooted in the use of static storage for the challenge_timestamp and challenge_count variables that are not scoped to individual network namespaces or per-socket contexts. The root cause is that these static variables are instantiated once system-wide rather than being isolated per network namespace, so their counter state is shared across all network stacks running on the same host. An attacker with the ability to send a modest flood of out-of-window TCP ACK packets, or access to an unprivileged local container network namespace, can increment the shared challenge_count value to exceed the sysctl_tcp_challenge_ack_limit threshold within a single jiffy interval. This action will block all valid challenge ACK generation across the entire host for the remainder of that second, breaking standard TCP connection sequence validation checks and causing widespread legitimate new connection failures or unhandled stale connection drops across all hosted network environments.

This code contains a critical uninitialized memory access vulnerability stemming from the failure to assign valid values to the local variables mask_isolation_id and mask_effect_id before their use. The two variables are declared on the stack with no initial value and passed by value to the CreateOrReuseSynthesizedClipLayer function, meaning the function cannot write valid output values back to the local stack variables of the caller. When the code later invokes mask_isolation_id.ToInternalValue and mask_effect_id.ToInternalValue to assign the stable_id fields of newly created effect nodes, it reads uninitialized stack memory that contains arbitrary untrusted or corrupted data. An attacker who can manipulate the contents of the uninitialized stack region at the point of this function call can trigger out-of-bounds property tree accesses, corrupt internal compositor state, achieve arbitrary read or write primitives on the heap, and ultimately execute arbitrary code within the privileged browser rendering process.

This code exhibits a cross-translation-unit static initialization order vulnerability that arises from the unguarded dependency of the local static root EffectPaintPropertyNode on the results of TransformPaintPropertyNode::Root and ClipPaintPropertyNode::Root. The C++ language specification does not define the initialization sequence for function-local static variables that reside in separate compilation units, so there is no guarantee the referenced transform and clip root nodes will be fully constructed before being passed to EffectPaintPropertyNode::Create. An attacker can trigger this undefined behavior by forcing early invocation of EffectPaintPropertyNode::Root during a phase of execution that precedes the initialization of the dependent static root objects, resulting in access to uninitialized heap or stack memory. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to corrupted rendering state, out of bounds memory reads and writes, and ultimately arbitrary code execution when processing untrusted graphical or web content.

This C code from the Linux kernel mount subsystem contains an unpaired unlock vulnerability that corrupts internal kernel locking state. The root cause occurs when IS_MNT_SHARED(dest_mnt) evaluates to true and propagate_mnt returns a non-zero error code, as the subsequent error handling jump to the out_cleanup_ids label executes unlock_mount_hash even though the mount hash lock was never acquired in this execution path. A local privileged attacker can trigger this invalid state by initiating a recursive mount operation on a shared mount point under controlled low memory conditions to force propagate_mnt to return an error after populating the tree_list structure. This unpaired unlock breaks the kernel's lock depth tracking, enabling unintended concurrent access to protected mount subsystem structures that can lead to kernel memory corruption, privilege escalation, or full system compromise.

This mkvparser ReadUInt function contains an out of bounds read vulnerability that arises from the absence of a validation check ensuring the computed len value does not cause the subsequent sequential read operations to exceed the bounds of the input media buffer. The root cause is that the code does not compare the sum of the initial pos value and the computed len value against the total remaining size of the underlying input buffer before issuing repeated read requests for the remaining bytes of the EBML variable length integer. An attacker can trigger this vulnerability by supplying a maliciously crafted MKV file where a valid 8 byte EBML integer is placed at an offset near the end of the media buffer, such that the 7 additional read operations required to fetch the full integer extend past the end of the allocated memory region. Successful exploitation of this issue can result in leakage of sensitive adjacent heap memory contents back to the attacker, unexpected application crashes due to access of unmapped memory pages, and potential remote arbitrary code execution through carefully manipulated adjacent memory contents.

This C code parsing Rock Ridge symbolic link entries for ISO 9660 filesystems contains a critical unvalidated integer overflow vulnerability during calculation of symlink target length. The root cause is the absence of upper bounds checks on cumulative increments to symlink_len and inode->i_size within the SIG('S', 'L') processing block, as the code repeatedly adds values derived from untrusted slp->len fields directly to the size counter without verifying the total does not exceed the maximum valid symlink length. An attacker can craft a malicious ISO 9660 disk image with specially constructed SL extension descriptors that trigger repeated unvalidated additions to the symlink size counter, wrapping the integer to a small value that causes the kernel to allocate an undersized buffer for the symlink target. When the kernel later copies the full untrusted symlink path data into this undersized buffer, it triggers a heap-based buffer overflow that can be exploited to achieve arbitrary kernel memory corruption, leading to local privilege escalation or full system compromise when the malicious image is mounted.

This code contains a time-of-check to time-of-use race condition vulnerability in the thread validation routine for the AcceleratedStaticBitmapImage class. The root cause is that the non-atomic boolean flag detach_thread_at_next_check_ is read and modified without any corresponding mutex lock or memory barrier, and the subsequent operations to detach the thread checker and validate the current thread identity can be interleaved by execution on a second untrusted thread. An attacker who can schedule concurrent execution of this method on multiple separate threads can trigger the narrow race window to completely bypass the valid thread identity enforcement. Successful exploitation allows an attacker to execute unsafe accelerated bitmap image rendering operations on an unexpected unapproved thread, leading to corrupted shared internal state, out of bounds memory access, arbitrary code execution, or widespread denial of service across the host application process.

This implementation of the AIO ring event read function contains a critical out-of-bounds kernel memory disclosure vulnerability. The root cause is that the function snapshots the shared ring tail value only once at the start of execution, immediately after acquiring the ring mutex, and never re-reads the updated tail value from the shared ring during the event processing loop, leading to stale bound checks that do not properly constrain the range of events that can be copied to user space. A local attacker can trigger this flaw by submitting a high volume of concurrent AIO completion events that increment the ring tail while the function is mid-execution, causing the loop to calculate an overly large avail count that exceeds the maximum valid index of the ctx->ring_pages array. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to leak arbitrary sensitive kernel memory contents, including credentials, function pointers, and private process data, which can be leveraged to achieve full local privilege escalation to root.

This code contains an unvalidated null pointer dereference vulnerability that arises when the input Element pointer e is null. The root cause is that the function directly invokes the hasTagName method on e without first validating that the pointer points to a valid allocated Element instance, even though the preceding isHTMLHtmlElement check may safely return false for a null input. An attacker who can pass a crafted null Element pointer to this function can trigger an immediate invalid memory read access when execution reaches the first e->hasTagName call. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability will result in an unexpected crash of the host web browser or rendering engine, leading to a denial of service condition that disrupts normal end user operation.

This code contains an unvalidated bounds vulnerability that leads to potential out-of-bounds memory read when processing maliciously crafted packet capture files or live captured network traffic. The root cause is the absence of any check that the l2info.cookie buffer holds enough bytes to fully populate the referenced juniper_ggsn_header structure, and no validation that the remaining bytes in the packet pointer p after advancing by l2info.header_len meet or exceed the untrusted l2info.length value passed to the ip_print and ip6_print functions. An attacker can trigger this flaw by supplying a malformed capture file with a truncated Juniper GGSN header that sets a small l2info.header_len and an arbitrarily large l2info.length value that is not bounded by the actual captured packet length. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to cause a crash of the running netdissect or tcpdump process, or leak sensitive adjacent memory contents from the process address space to disclose unintended internal process data.

This code contains a critical undefined behavior vulnerability stemming from improper handling of the switch statement default case. The root cause is that the NOTREACHED() macro is a debug-only assertion that is removed entirely from production release builds, and most modern C++ compilers interpret this marker as a guarantee that the default path can never be executed, enabling aggressive unsafe optimizations that eliminate adjacent implicit safety checks. An attacker that can trigger a notification type not explicitly enumerated in the switch cases will force execution down the unhandled default path, violating the compiler’s assumed invariants and triggering unintended optimized behavior. Successful exploitation can bypass critical security validation, corrupt adjacent heap or stack memory, redirect execution flow to arbitrary attacker controlled addresses, and achieve full remote code execution in the browser process.

This empty user-defined destructor for the BlockEntry class introduces a critical unmanaged resource release vulnerability if the BlockEntry type holds any dynamically allocated heap buffers, open file descriptors, or other operating system managed resources as member variables. This code contains a critical implicit return type vulnerability stemming from the omission of an explicit return type for the spnego_gss_get_mic_iov_length function, which relies on the obsolete C implicit int convention that defaults the function return to a 32-bit signed integer. This code contains a critical stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability stemming from the use of the unsafe sprintf function to write formatted output to the fixed 1024-byte stack-allocated pathName buffer. Successful exploitation lets the attacker corrupt adjacent stack memory, overwrite critical control flow data such as function return addresses, and achieve arbitrary code execution in the context of the vulnerable PDF processing application.

This code exhibits an uninitialized heap memory and missing shader data copy vulnerability in the long segmented shader continuation processing logic. This flaw allows an attacker to supply malformed or partially untrusted shader input to the underlying TGSI translation and GPU driver stack, leading to information disclosure of sensitive host process memory, arbitrary GPU code execution, and full guest to host privilege escalation.

This code contains an uninitialized kernel stack memory disclosure vulnerability stemming from implicit structure padding bytes that are not explicitly zeroed or initialized. A local unprivileged attacker can trigger this vulnerability by opening a netlink socket and sending a request to retrieve network device link information, which invokes this function to generate the response. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to read unintended arbitrary values from the kernel stack, which can expose sensitive internal kernel pointers or data that aids in bypassing standard kernel memory protections and executing further privilege escalation attacks.

The identified vulnerability is an out-of-bounds read flaw in the kernel command line concatenation logic for non-override CONFIG_CMDLINE_BOOL builds. The root cause arises from two sequential strlcat calls operating on the fixed-size builtin_cmdline buffer, both using the full COMMAND_LINE_SIZE value as their size limit, which produces a non-null-terminated intermediate string after appending the required leading space when the initial builtin_cmdline value is already at maximum valid length, leading the second strlcat to scan past the allocated buffer bounds to find a null terminator. This flaw can be triggered by a malicious or compromised bootloader that manipulates the embedded builtin_cmdline to fill its full buffer capacity without leaving space for the appended space character and trailing null. Exploitation of this vulnerability can result in sensitive kernel memory disclosure of adjacent uninitialized kernel data, unexpected system hang, or fatal kernel panic from access to unmapped physical memory pages during the out-of-bounds string scan.

This code implements a critical same-origin policy bypass vulnerability in the web media player's security validation routine. A remote attacker can trigger this flaw by manipulating media playback initialization flows to leave the data_source_ pointer unassigned or freed prior to this security check executing, which skips the intended cross-origin validation logic. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to access and exfiltrate sensitive content from cross-origin media resources that would otherwise be blocked, violating core web platform security guarantees and enabling unauthorized information disclosure from a victim user’s browser context.

This code contains a critical unvalidated pointer dereference vulnerability that can lead to unexpected process termination or arbitrary code execution. An attacker who can manipulate the thread local execution state to force GetCoordinatorBindingForCurrentThread to return a null or dangling pointer can trigger an out-of-bounds memory access when the subsequent method call on the invalid coordinator pointer executes. Successful exploitation of this flaw can result in a denial of service crash of the target process, and may allow an attacker to execute arbitrary attacker-controlled code or leak sensitive heap profiling metadata if the memory at the invalid pointer address is under malicious control.

This code exhibits an unvalidated pointer dereference security vulnerability rooted in the complete absence of input validation for the `struct timespec *value` input parameter. The function directly writes to `value->tv_sec` and `value->tv_nsec` immediately after calculating the nanosecond value, with no check to confirm the `value` pointer references a valid, writable memory region. An attacker can trigger this flaw by calling the function with a NULL or arbitrary controlled non-address value for the `value` parameter, rather than a pointer to a properly allocated timespec structure. Successful exploitation will result in a fatal memory access fault that crashes the hosting process or kernel to cause a denial of service, and may allow arbitrary memory corruption if the attacker supplies a pointer that targets a sensitive, attacker-chosen writable memory location.

This code contains an undefined behavior signed integer overflow vulnerability during the MSB to host byte order conversion step when constructing the 32-bit long return value. The root cause is that the unsigned char elements of the buffer array are implicitly promoted to default signed int prior to execution of the bitwise left shift operations, so when buffer[0] holds a value greater than 127, the operation buffer[0] << 24 produces a signed integer with a value exceeding the maximum permitted for a 32-bit signed int, which is explicitly undefined under the C language standard. An attacker can trigger this condition by supplying a crafted serialized input where the first byte of the target 4-byte long property has the most significant bit set, easily bypassing the existing length check that only verifies at least 4 bytes are available for reading. Successful exploitation can lead to unintended integer value corruption, incorrect sign extension, or unexpected program control flow that may enable downstream memory corruption or incorrect access control decisions depending on how the returned signed integer value is consumed by the calling application.

An attacker who can trigger execution of the KillProcess function on an arbitrary unvetted thread can trigger race conditions that corrupt the internal state of the shared objects, leading to invalid handle access or use-after-free conditions. Successful exploitation of this flaw can allow an attacker to terminate arbitrary unintended system processes, leak sensitive kernel object information, or achieve local privilege escalation on the target host.

This Linux kernel key management function contains a critical use-after-free vulnerability stemming from improper handling of the user-provided description pointer. A local unprivileged attacker can trigger this flaw by passing a userland description pointer that is deliberately freed or mutated in parallel execution after the relevant syscall is invoked, leading the kernel to operate on unvalidated or deallocated memory. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows an attacker to leak sensitive kernel stack or heap data, corrupt adjacent kernel memory structures, and escalate privileges to obtain full unrestricted administrative access on the target system.

This code contains a critical kernel stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability rooted in the use of an unvalidated variable-length array allocated directly on the kernel stack for the 'state' buffer. The code declares the stack buffer 'state' with a size returned directly from crypto_ahash_statesize without imposing any upper bound check, allowing a malicious or misconfigured cryptographic algorithm to return an excessively large state size that far exceeds the limited available kernel stack memory. When the subsequent call to crypto_ahash_export writes the full algorithm state data into this undersized stack buffer, the operation overwrites adjacent critical kernel stack structures including return addresses and saved register values. An attacker with the ability to register a malicious custom hash algorithm can trigger this flaw to escalate privileges, execute arbitrary kernel code, or crash the entire system to cause a permanent denial of service condition.

This code exhibits a critical unvalidated input pointer vulnerability that arises from the complete lack of sanity checks on the incoming JNIEnv* env parameter before it is passed directly to the RegisterNativesImpl call. The root cause is the implicit assumption that the caller will always provide a valid, properly initialized JNI environment pointer, with no checks for NULL values or corrupted memory addresses. A remote or local attacker controlling the parameters passed to this function can supply an invalid pointer referencing arbitrary memory locations, triggering unintended memory access operations within the subsequent RegisterNativesImpl logic. Successful exploitation of this flaw can lead to unexpected application denial of service, disclosure of sensitive in-memory process data, or full arbitrary code execution under the privileges of the targeted host process.

This code contains a null pointer dereference vulnerability that arises because the only validation of the url and title pointer parameters is performed via a DCHECK macro, which is excluded from standard non-debug release builds. This code contains a critical unvalidated pointer vulnerability that stems from the lack of input checks for the name parameter passed to the path_name function. This code exhibits a critical dangling pointer and unintended use-after-free vulnerability that arises from returning a raw non-owning pointer to an object managed by the std::unique_ptr member browser_client_. Successful exploitation of this flaw allows an attacker to access and manipulate freed memory, corrupt adjacent heap metadata, and ultimately achieve arbitrary code execution with the full privilege level of the running web browser process.

The identified security vulnerability is a broken IDN homograph spoof protection implementation caused by incorrectly constructed Unicode sets and malformed custom transliteration rules. The root cause is that the cyrillic_letters_latin_alike_ UnicodeSet is initialized with a garbled UTF8 string that mixes unrelated CJK ideographs, literal ASCII text en, and partial misrepresented Cyrillic glyphs that fail to capture the full set of Latin-lookalike Cyrillic characters, while the custom transliteration rules for confusable characters map arbitrary unrelated CJK characters to basic Latin ASCII letters instead of only valid confusable non-ASCII characters. An attacker can trigger this flaw by registering IDN domain names that use valid Latin-lookalike Cyrillic characters not captured by the incomplete cyrillic_letters_latin_alike_ set, or CJK characters incorrectly mapped to common Latin letters by the flawed transliteration rules, to create homograph spoof domains that visually mimic trusted legitimate domain names. This empty implementation of the Compositor OnFirstSurfaceActivation callback contains a critical missing security control vulnerability that stems from the complete omission of all required input validation and authorization logic for incoming SurfaceInfo data. This function contains a critical unsigned integer overflow vulnerability that leads to a heap-based buffer overflow when processing untrusted RPC package input. The root cause is the complete lack of validation for the user-controlled pkg->ext_size and pkg->body_size fields, which are added to the fixed RPC_PKG_HEAD_SIZE to calculate the final pkg_size, allowing an attacker to supply large size values that cause the sum to wrap around to a small, severely under-estimated value. This code contains an unvalidated pointer dereference security vulnerability that stems from missing null check logic for the pointer returned by GetSpeechSynthesisLibrary. This implementation of the pin_remove function contains a critical unvalidated double list deletion vulnerability that can result in severe memory corruption. This operation will write unintended pointer values to arbitrary adjacent memory locations, potentially allowing the attacker to escalate privileges, execute arbitrary code in kernel context, or crash the running system to produce a denial of service.

This YARA virtual machine execution code contains a critical out-of-bounds memory access vulnerability that affects the internal fixed-size stack-allocated mem array.
